title: Indexes & Search
summary: Finding the needle without scanning the haystack. 6 building blocks drilled by recall: the signal that says reach for one, what it costs, how it breaks, which sibling rules it out, and what it is doing across the canonical problems.
keyTakeaways: Inverted Index / Search — A term-to-document mapping built ahead of time, so full-text and faceted queries are lookups rather than scans.
Vector Search — Approximate nearest-neighbour lookup over embeddings, retrieving by semantic similarity instead of by keyword.
Ranking — Ordering a candidate set by a score — recency, affinity, engagement, relevance — usually as a cheap retrieval stage followed by an expensive scoring stage.
Geospatial Index — Mapping 2-D coordinates onto a 1-D key that preserves locality — geohash, quadtree or S2 — so 'what is near me' becomes a range scan.
Bloom Filter — A compact probabilistic set that answers 'definitely not present' or 'probably present', trading exactness for tiny memory.
Trie / Autocomplete — A prefix tree with top-K completions precomputed at each node, so a keystroke returns suggestions in a single traversal.

questions.prompt: Inverted Index / Search vs Trie / Autocomplete vs Vector Search — what decides between them?
points: Trie / Autocomplete — For prefix matching specifically, a trie is far cheaper than a general search engine.
Vector Search — When the match should be semantic rather than lexical.
Inverted Index / Search — A term-to-document mapping built ahead of time, so full-text and faceted queries are lookups rather than scans.
questions.answer: Trie / Autocomplete: For prefix matching specifically, a trie is far cheaper than a general search engine. Vector Search: When the match should be semantic rather than lexical.

questions.prompt: Inverted Index / Search appears in 4 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a Typeahead / Autocomplete Service — The prefix-to-completions structure that turns each keystroke into a lookup rather than a scan over the query log.
Design a RAG / Semantic Search System — Keyword retrieval running alongside vector search, because hybrid retrieval consistently beats either one alone on real queries.
Design a Search Engine — The inverted index is the system: term → posting list is what makes query time independent of corpus size.

Design a Sanctions Screening System — Alias, transliteration and spelling expansion turn 40K sanctioned entities into millions of searchable strings, so candidate generation runs over an n-gram index rather than the entity list.

questions.prompt: Ranking appears in 6 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a News Feed — Orders the assembled timeline by recency, affinity and engagement rather than pure chronology — the second half of the feed problem after fan-out.
Design a RAG / Semantic Search System — Reranks vector-retrieved candidates before they reach the model, because approximate-nearest-neighbour recall is not the same thing as relevance.
Design a Search Engine — Scores matching documents so the top-K is worth reading. Retrieval finds candidates; ranking is what makes the result page useful.
Design a Short-Form Video Feed — Drives the entire product. The feed is not a follow graph but a ranked stream, so the ranker IS the short-form video experience.
Design a Content Moderation Pipeline — Prioritises the review queue so the most likely violations and the highest-reach content reach a human moderator first.

Design a Sanctions Screening System — Scoring the surviving candidates is where date of birth, nationality and identifiers separate a genuine hit from a common surname, and it produces three bands rather than a boolean.

questions.prompt: Bloom Filter vs Deduplication vs Cache — what decides between them?
points: Deduplication — When you need certainty, an exact content-address index is the honest answer.
Cache — A negative cache stores known-absent keys exactly, at higher memory cost.
Bloom Filter — A compact probabilistic set that answers 'definitely not present' or 'probably present', trading exactness for tiny memory.
questions.answer: Deduplication: When you need certainty, an exact content-address index is the honest answer. Cache: A negative cache stores known-absent keys exactly, at higher memory cost.

questions.prompt: Bloom Filter appears in 5 of the canonical design problems. Name as many as you can, and say what it is doing in each.
points: Design a URL Shortener — Answers 'has this short code been issued' without a lookup, turning most collision checks into a memory read.
Design a Web Crawler — The seen-URL check — the canonical use, asked billions of times, where a false positive only costs a skipped page.
Design a Distributed Cache — Avoids a network hop for keys a node certainly does not hold, which matters when the miss costs a round trip to the origin.
Design a File Sync / Object Storage Service — Tests whether a chunk already exists before uploading it, so the dedup path avoids a round trip for genuinely new content.
Design a Distributed Key-Value Store — Sits in front of each SSTable so a read skips files that certainly do not hold the key.

questions.prompt: Trie / Autocomplete vs Inverted Index / Search vs Cache — what decides between them?
points: Inverted Index / Search — A general search engine with an edge-ngram analyser, when you want fuzziness and are willing to pay for it.
Cache — Popular prefixes dominate the distribution; caching their results absorbs most requests before the trie.
Trie / Autocomplete — A prefix tree with top-K completions precomputed at each node, so a keystroke returns suggestions in a single traversal.
